full_judgment: 8. In answering the incidental question which cropped up during the course of arguments as to whether the applicant can at all raise any objection as to the sufficiency of the period of notice, Mr. Khonker emphatically asserted that the plaintiff-respondent must succeed on the strength of her own case. For, he mentioned though the defendant-appellant did not rely on the kabuliyat, it is the plaintiff-respondent's cast that the kabuliyat in question was executed by the defendant-appellant. Mention may be made that in her written statement it was alleged that the kabuliyat was obtained by fraud and was not, therefore, a valid document. In support of the principle that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his own case, Mr. Khondker cited the case of Jagadish Narian Vs. Nawab Said Ahmed Khan, (1945) 50 CWN PC 477. The principle, though elementary is no doubt important but when the very foundation of the plaintiff-respondent's claim has totally been denied by the defendant-appellant who dismissed the kabuliyat as a fraudulent transaction, it is difficult to concede that the defendant-appellant should be allowed to rely on a point whose validity depends upon the acceptance of the document itself, which can give rise to such point. Expediency is not an unknown phenomenon in the legal arena, but the principles of approbation and reapprobation are also equally well known. A party to a Suit after taking an exact stand in his plain or written" statement cannot so readily be allowed to depart from it on the ground that his opponent admitted the position which was opposite to his stand, Justice and expediency cannot go together.
